Middle East & Africa | The Levant’s toughest knot In his office in downtown Beirut, Amer Bisat looks to the past to sketch a hopeful vision of the future. Lebanon was once the region’s premier entrepôt, a hub for banking, tourism and trade; perhaps it can be so again. “If reconstruction ev...
item.content:encoded:
Lebanon’s president wants to enlist Donald Trump in rebuilding the country

Middle East & Africa | The Levant’s toughest knot


In his office in downtown Beirut, Amer Bisat looks to the past to sketch a hopeful vision of the future. Lebanon was once the region’s premier entrepôt, a hub for banking, tourism and trade; perhaps it can be so again. “If reconstruction ever starts in Syria, for example, Lebanese ports might be part of that,” says the economy minister. He also hopes to woo Gulf states keen to lay pipelines and fibre-optic cables that bypass the Strait of Hormuz. “The region is being redrawn in many ways,” says Mr Bisat, “and Lebanon has a huge role to play.”

A kilometre away stands an eerie reminder of Lebanon’s more recent history. The port of Beirut was wrecked in 2020 by one of the largest non-nuclear explosions in history. Fearful of exposing their own corruption and negligence, politicians have long stalled an investigation into the blast, which killed more than 200 people. The port has yet to be fully rebuilt. Families of victims petitioned to keep a damaged grain silo standing as a makeshift memorial, a Daliesque edifice frozen in mid-collapse.

As Joseph Aoun, Lebanon’s president, met Donald Trump in Washington on July 21st, it also stood as a warning to would-be investors—one of many in Lebanon today. The period since mass anti-government protests in 2019 has been the worst for the country since the end of its long civil war in 1990. It has endured the port explosion, a financial crisis and almost three years of war with Israel.

For most of this time it muddled through with a series of caretaker prime ministers and, for more than two years, no president. The vacuum ended in January 2025, when parliament selected Mr Aoun. Days later Nawaf Salam was named prime minister. They make an odd couple. Mr Aoun, bald and broad, is a career soldier, while the bespectacled, bookish Mr Salam is an academic and diplomat who spent much of his life abroad.

Both are political outsiders in a country long dominated by a crop of ex-warlords. In their inaugural speeches they pledged to disarm Hizbullah, the Iran-backed Shia militia that has long defied the government’s authority, and to implement long-overdue reforms. The watchword for both was sovereignty: no longer would Lebanon be defined by foreign meddling and state weakness.

Eighteen months on, their record is mixed. They have taken some laudable decisions, from proscribing Hizbullah’s military wing to passing laws that should help unlock an IMF deal. Implementing decisions is another matter, and the forces of inertia are strong. Lebanon’s twin crises have become a Gordian knot. It will struggle to attract donors and investors unless it takes on Hizbullah, yet its strategy for doing so relies on those same donors and investors. Untangling the knot will mean doing everything at once—disarmament, reform and reconstruction—in a country that has long struggled to do anything at all.

Much of Mr Aoun’s conversation with Mr Trump focused on Hizbullah. The militia dragged Lebanon into war on October 8th 2023, when it fired rockets at Israel in support of Hamas, the Palestinian militant group that had just massacred around 1,200 people. Though America imposed a ceasefire in November 2024, Israel continued regular air strikes in Lebanon (Hizbullah was too degraded to retaliate). All-out war resumed in March this year, when the militia attacked Israel on Iran’s behalf.

The cost has been enormous. The government estimates that the most recent fighting caused $3bn-4bn in direct damage, on top of $8.5bn from the previous round (around 40% of gdp in total). It will also lop 7-8% off Lebanon’s output this year; Mr Bisat expects a recession.

Israel has razed villages in the south and occupied a swathe of the region. Hizbullah’s death toll is heavy. In eastern Lebanon’s Bekaa Valley, your correspondent counted a dozen posters announcing the deaths of Hizbullah fighters in one Shia village, home to perhaps 1,500 people. That is only a partial accounting: the group has yet to recover and identify all of its dead, and some families have been told not to mourn publicly. It is plausible, then, that 1-2% of the village has been killed fighting Israel since 2023. In the south, black-clad women spend their days visiting one home after another to pay condolences.

For decades Hizbullah has been a state within a state. It runs an extensive welfare network of schools, hospitals and youth programmes; it even operates a parallel banking system, which helped shield its supporters from the financial crash. These activities bred a loyalty that the state itself could not match—but the latest war has strained it. The group cannot afford to rebuild ruined areas. Its bank, al-Qard al-Hassan, has faced cash shortages.

Many of its constituents are exhausted. Some are concerned by Iran’s growing sway over the group. In March the Lebanese government tried to expel the Iranian ambassador, accusing him of using his post to support Hizbullah on behalf of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (irgc), the Iranian regime’s praetorians. He refused to leave. In June Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, the speaker of Iran’s parliament, praised Lebanon for offering 4,000 “martyrs” in support of his country. His comments outraged many Lebanese.

Officials close to Mr Aoun thus see an opportunity to flip the script. “We hope to have two clear scenes,” says one: “Hizbullah killing your sons for the Iranian interest… and on the other hand, we have a Lebanese state keen to protect them, to reconstruct their villages and homes.” It is a creative approach, more carrot than stick. But it faces three big obstacles.

First, and most difficult, is how to disarm Hizbullah. The group refuses to comply and is fond of threatening a new civil war if anyone tries to take its weapons. Nonetheless, last August the cabinet agreed on a plan to gradually do just that, and in March it declared the group’s military wing illegal. Several dozen people have since been arrested for transporting arms. In June Israel and Lebanon signed a deal that commits the latter to deploy its army in southern Lebanon.

But the army is in no state to force the issue. Hizbullah is still better equipped. Though defence spending has more than tripled since 2021, most of the budget goes to wages, not weapons. Some officers are thought to be sympathetic to Hizbullah. Nor are courts much of a deterrent. One illegal-weapons case in March ended with Hizbullah members being fined just 900,000 Lebanese lira ($10).

Second is how to ensure Israeli withdrawal: the state will not look credible unless it does. The deal with Israel has begun with two “pilot zones” (see map), a proof of concept that will show the Lebanese army can move in and Israeli troops can pull out. Officials in Beirut complain that one of these zones includes villages that Israel never occupied in the first place. Meanwhile, it continues periodic air strikes in the south. The lawnmower buzz of an Israeli surveillance drone is ever-present background noise in much of Lebanon, even at the hilltop presidential palace in Baabda.

The final question is who will pay to rebuild. The last time Lebanon’s friends organised a donor conference, in 2018, they pledged $11bn but never disbursed the money because the government failed to implement required reforms. America no longer believes in foreign aid. Mr Aoun hopes Mr Trump will help him drum up American investment. Yet the same concerns that put off donors before may spook would-be investors today.

Lebanon’s crises overlap. The financial crash was decades in the making—the result of a state-run Ponzi scheme meant to finance massive deficits and keep the currency pegged at 1,500 to the dollar. When bank deposits flattened off in 2019, the scheme collapsed. Lenders in effect halted foreign-currency withdrawals. The following years were marked by hyperinflation, rapid depreciation and political paralysis. Though Lebanon reached a tentative four-year, $3bn deal with the IMF in April 2022, the fund’s board never put it to a final vote. Again, lack of reform was the issue: the banks have powerful allies in parliament, who blocked any attempt at restructuring.

If things look better now, it is only because they were so bad before. The currency has settled at just shy of 90,000 to the dollar, 98% below the peg. Annual inflation has fallen from a peak of 221% in 2023 to 15% last year, still among the highest in the world. At $30bn, the economy is about half its pre-crisis size (it was $55bn in 2018). Depositors are still mostly locked out of their accounts, able to withdraw $800 or less per month.

Mr Salam’s government has taken some meaningful steps. In April 2025 it eased the bank-secrecy law, a longtime IMF demand. Three months later it passed another bill that lets the state restructure or liquidate insolvent lenders. But it has yet to approve the most consequential (and controversial) piece of legislation: the so-called “gap law”, which would apportion roughly $80bn in losses between banks, depositors and the state.

Under a draft proposal approved by the cabinet in December, small depositors would be able to recover up to $100,000 over four years. Mr Salam says that will cover 85% of account-holders. The rest will receive asset-backed securities that may take as long as 20 years to pay out. This plan is unworkable, however. Payments to depositors would cost at least $22bn over four years, far more than the state or the Banque du Liban, the central bank, can afford. Three sources say the four-year timeline will have to be extended.

Fixing the banks is only a first step. Lebanon also needs new sources of growth. Mr Bisat points to start-ups that are making hardware for robotics and AI data centres. With its strong universities, cheap labour and entrepreneurial culture, Lebanon has some comparative advantages. “There are certain services that we excel at…things like high-level tourism, high-level design, construction services, consultancies,” he says.

For all its talented businesspeople, though, Lebanon has a terrible business climate. The war is one problem. Zombie banks are another: the economy has lost its financial infrastructure. Lending has collapsed. Credit to the private sector has plunged from 107% of gdp in 2018 to less than 20% today.

Lebanon’s infrastructure is in a parlous state. The state-run electric company can supply only a few hours of power per day. Businesses pay for a private generator subscription—which, at $0.48 per kilowatt-hour, is nearly three times pricier than the global average. Expensive deliveries of water from private lorries supplement erratic public utilities. Firms, lumbered with slower broadband speeds than in Somalia, are desperate for Starlink to launch so they can ditch the lousy state-run telecoms monopoly.

Little money exists to fix any of this. The government ran a fiscal surplus of 2% of gdp last year, and despite the war it expects to post a narrower one in 2026. Yet more than half of revenue is spent on wages and pensions. Fouad Makhzoumi, an mp and aspiring prime minister, estimates there are 340,000 people in the public sector, almost 10% of Lebanon’s citizen population. “We asked the government to tell us how many employees we have,” he says. “Until now, we have no idea.”

Ministers take care to distinguish between themselves and “the system”. It seems an odd distinction: surely the cabinet is at the centre of a parliamentary system. But it is an accurate one. Hizbullah still controls the guns. Bankers and their allies can still block a financial overhaul, and confessional chieftains parcel out the spoils of the state. The system is built to outlast would-be reformers.

Sovereignty is not just about the Israeli drone whirring overhead or the Iranian ambassador who refuses to leave. It is also about freeing the state from an establishment that feeds on its weakness. “This is a system that has ways of saving itself, and that should not be underestimated,” says one elder statesman. For now, the ruined silo by the port seems like a symbol for Lebanon itself: neither fallen nor rebuilt but caught mid-collapse. ■

item.title: For Russians, the war feels closer than ever before
item.description:
Europe

Europe | Up in smoke Eight civilians lay dead. More than 80 were injured. Columns of black smoke billowed from the wreckage. On July 18th Ukrainian drones hit two giant warehouses belonging to Wildberries, Russia’s largest online retailer, in Moscow and Tambov, some 475km south-east of the capi...
item.content:encoded:
For Russians, the war feels closer than ever before

Europe | Up in smoke


Eight civilians lay dead. More than 80 were injured. Columns of black smoke billowed from the wreckage. On July 18th Ukrainian drones hit two giant warehouses belonging to Wildberries, Russia’s largest online retailer, in Moscow and Tambov, some 475km south-east of the capital. The bombs are thought to have destroyed some 150bn roubles ($1.9bn) worth of consumer goods. Four days later Ukraine bombed two more warehouses in south-west Russia. One woman was killed.

Volodymyr Zelensky, Ukraine’s president, said that soldiers and volunteers use Wildberries to buy military-related goods such as drone components and bulletproof vests. But he also signalled revenge. The attacks, he said, were a “response to Russian strikes on our civilian infrastructure and on our cities and communities”. They followed strikes on facilities belonging to Nova Poshta, a Ukrainian postal and logistics company, which Russia says are also used for military purposes.

Ukraine’s attacks on refineries, which have caused fuel shortages across the country, were already bringing the war home. The latest strikes further undermine the notion that the fighting will stay confined to the battlefield in Ukraine and drive home the Russian authorities’ failure to defend their own people. “Those black columns of smoke have become part of everyday life,” says one Muscovite. Wildberries has millions of customers. Hundreds of thousands of businesses use it to sell everything from socks to smartphones (not to mention body armour and fibre-optic cable). “The attacks on Wildberries warehouses have affected nearly 100% of the population in one way or another: some physically, some financially, and others psychologically,” says Elena Panfilova, a Russian political scientist.

Merchants who sell their wares on the site filled social media with videos and posts. One mother from a small town posted on Instagram: “I made everything with my own hands...and then this happened. Everything fell apart. What am I supposed to do now?” Natalia Plonke, who sells cosmetics, said: “The risks are being shifted onto us. The losses are becoming ours, too. It’s only going to get worse.” But for Wildberries the attack was not a complete surprise. Two weeks earlier the company revised the terms of its contracts with merchants, disclaiming responsibility for war-related losses.

Russian military bloggers have long lamented the apathy of Russians who tried to ignore the war. Responding to the latest strikes, some pro-war nationalists sounded almost gleeful. “From the point of view of getting people involved, [these attacks] are a plus,” said one commentator. In fact such strikes may make Russians more resentful towards the war. In the Samara region a veteran recently tried flashing his credentials to get petrol without queuing. Angry motorists beat him up.

Public discontent is rising. According to VCIOM, a pollster close to the Kremlin, satisfaction with government policies has fallen from 45% in January to 21% in June. The number of people who think Russia is heading in the wrong direction has doubled from 17% to 35% in the past year, says Levada, an independent pollster. President Vladimir Putin’s own approval ratings are falling, too, though from a high level.

In Moscow campaign posters reading “Za Putina” (“For Putin”)—complete with the Latin letter “Z”, symbolising the war—are now commonplace. Parliamentary elections are two months away. Any politician who speaks against the war has been excluded from standing. The Kremlin will declare whatever result it wants.

But the Kremlin cannot control how Russians feel. Most want the war to end. News broadcasts are leaving out information about Ukraine’s drone attacks, further eroding trust in television—one of Mr Putin’s levers of power. While 56% of Russians still mention television as their main source of information, only 37% say they trust it. In the past, Mr Putin brought the war to their TV screens. Now he has brought it into their daily lives. ■

item.title: Spain’s team embodies footballing values FIFA has betrayed
item.description:
Europe

Europe | The World Cup Less than 24 hours after Spain’s victory over Argentina in the World Cup final, Madrid turned out to congratulate the team as they paraded in an open-top bus. “Champions of the World”, sang the crowds. The government reckoned 1.8m people (in a city of 3.5m) attended the c...
item.content:encoded:
Spain’s team embodies footballing values FIFA has betrayed

Europe | The World Cup


Less than 24 hours after Spain’s victory over Argentina in the World Cup final, Madrid turned out to congratulate the team as they paraded in an open-top bus. “Champions of the World”, sang the crowds. The government reckoned 1.8m people (in a city of 3.5m) attended the celebration, many waiting hours in suffocating heat.

La Roja (The Reds) embody Spanish virtues that casual visitors often overlook: modesty, hard work and above all teamwork and unity. Their success is based on denying the opposition possession of the ball, and close control and probing inter-passing when attacking. In an era of flamboyant sporting superstars, Spain’s most influential figure was Rodrigo “Rodri” Hernández, an unobtrusive midfield general who was named the World Cup’s best player.

The team represents national cohesion in a country of fragmented political geography. The squad included nine Catalans and three Basques. Lamine Yamal and Nico Williams, two rising stars, are the children of African immigrants. Until recently, many Catalans and Basques were ambivalent towards La Roja. Now many seem enthusiastic. The final’s audience share on TV in the Basque country was 84%, just below the national average of 87%. The only acts of intolerance were by Bilbao’s mayor, a Basque nationalist, who refused to install an outdoor screen for the final, and extremists who tried to sabotage one set up by a conservative party.

On the pitch, Spain’s victory was one for the values of football. Argentina kicked and shoved. A less indulgent referee would have handed out more than the single red card they received during the match. The punches they threw at their opponents after the final whistle will be investigated by FIFA, the sport’s governing body.

This World Cup was marked by innovations. Expansion from 32 to 48 teams was on balance a success.  Not so crass commercialisation, with advertising breaks disguised as “hydration breaks” and a lengthy half-time show alien to the sport’s traditions. Football is also supposed to be free of political interference. But FIFA drew criticism when it rescinded a red card from an American player after Donald Trump called Gianni Infantino, the organisation’s boss. In the final, Mr Trump was backing Argentina, an ally. Too bad: the filigree football of Spain, whom he has called a “terrible partner”, prevailed. ■

item.title: 代孕丑闻让德国保守派陷入动荡
item.description:
Europe

欧洲 | 施潘出局 延斯·施潘（Jens Spahn）——直到最近还是德国基民盟（CDU）及其姊妹党基社盟（CSU）的议会党团领袖——缺乏敏锐的政治直觉。7月15日，施潘在社交媒体和接受小报《图片报》采访时表示，他和丈夫通过代孕在美国生下了一个男婴。对他而言不幸的是，这在选民眼中像是厚颜无耻的虚伪。代孕在德国是非法的，而作为保守派的前卫生部长，施潘曾主张应维持这一禁令。三天后，他辞职了。 施潘的离开对总理弗里德里希·默茨（Friedrich Merz）来说很棘手。两人关系并不密切：2018年，施潘曾与默茨竞争基民盟领导权。但施潘与其社民党对手马蒂亚斯·米尔施（Matthias Miersch...
item.content:encoded:
代孕丑闻让德国保守派陷入动荡

欧洲 | 施潘出局

延斯·施潘（Jens Spahn）——直到最近还是德国基民盟（CDU）及其姊妹党基社盟（CSU）的议会党团领袖——缺乏敏锐的政治直觉。7月15日，施潘在社交媒体和接受小报《图片报》采访时表示，他和丈夫通过代孕在美国生下了一个男婴。对他而言不幸的是，这在选民眼中像是厚颜无耻的虚伪。代孕在德国是非法的，而作为保守派的前卫生部长，施潘曾主张应维持这一禁令。三天后，他辞职了。

施潘的离开对总理弗里德里希·默茨（Friedrich Merz）来说很棘手。两人关系并不密切：2018年，施潘曾与默茨竞争基民盟领导权。但施潘与其社民党对手马蒂亚斯·米尔施（Matthias Miersch）关系良好，且善于管理两党之间争吵不休的执政联盟。两人促成了一项全面的改革方案，即7月1日敲定的34点“增长与就业计划”。其中最重要的内容是对陷入困境的公共养老金体系进行改革，并为中低收入者提供税收减免。如果政府要想在9月德国东部各州的地方选举中有任何机会阻止极右翼的德国选择党（AfD），就必须推出这些措施。没有施潘的谈判手腕，执政联盟可能重新陷入混乱。

默茨迟迟未能理解施潘的声明引发的强烈抗议。在公共广播公司ZDF的年度“夏季访谈”节目中，总理暗示，公众的愤怒之所以如此强烈，是因为施潘这个人本身就充满争议且丑闻缠身。施潘是德国最不受欢迎的政治人物之一。2020年，他从他曾担任监事会成员的一家银行获得了购买别墅的贷款。疫情期间，他将一份高价口罩合同授予了雇有其丈夫的公司（卫生部否认给予优待）。许多人也不喜欢他与MAGA（让美国再次伟大）圈子的联系：他与前美国大使理查德·格伦内尔（Richard Grenell）以及极右翼科技大亨彼得·蒂尔（Peter Thiel）关系友好。

默茨想尽快摆脱施潘事件。7月29日，基民盟和基社盟的议员将中断假期，前往柏林投票选举施潘的继任者。据媒体报道，联邦总理府部长托尔斯滕·弗赖（Thorsten Frei）将接替他的职位。“他在议员中很受欢迎，尽管他没有施潘那样擅长让他们听话的策略思维，”智库贝塔斯曼基金会（Bertelsmann Foundation）的凯瑟琳·克吕弗·阿什布鲁克（Cathryn Clüver Ashbrook）表示。弗赖可能的继任者是卫生部长尼娜·瓦尔肯（Nina Warken）。调任她将需要进行内阁改组。

目前尚不清楚人事变动能否重振默茨低迷的支持率。他可能会尝试通过更换执政联盟中几位基民盟或基社盟的部长来重启政府。选民们不太喜欢交通部长帕特里克·施尼德（Patrick Schnieder）和经济部长卡塔琳娜·赖歇（Katherina Reiche）。施尼德因国家铁路服务德国铁路公司臭名昭著的延误而受到指责。赖歇则因被认为与化石燃料行业关系密切，且未能拿出有效的产业政策而不受欢迎。■

item.title: Ukraine’s new military commander aims to fight a more modern war
item.description:
Europe

Europe | The butcher’s bill RENOWNED GENERALS from George Patton, who strutted about in cavalry boots and carried two ivory-handled pistols, to the ascetic Bernard Montgomery, understood that their troops’ morale depends a lot on the image they project of themselves. Few will have taken the job...
item.content:encoded:
Ukraine’s new military commander aims to fight a more modern war

Europe | The butcher’s bill


RENOWNED GENERALS from George Patton, who strutted about in cavalry boots and carried two ivory-handled pistols, to the ascetic Bernard Montgomery, understood that their troops’ morale depends a lot on the image they project of themselves. Few will have taken the job with the legendary status of Mykhailo Drapaty (pictured), who was named the commander-in-chief of Ukraine’s armed forces on July 21st, replacing Oleksandr Syrsky.

Many hope his appointment will lead to the modernisation of Ukraine’s armed forces. Though they have shown an unexpected talent for innovation and adaptability in the years since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, they have been unable entirely to shake off the stultifying rigidity of their old Soviet-era command structures.

General Drapaty, aged 43, first rose to fame as a young major in 2014 when Russia-backed separatists tried to seize Mariupol, a city on the south-east coast. Leading from the front in command of a column of four armoured vehicles, he smashed through rebel barricades and into the city. Later that year he led his battalion on a raid along the Russian border to cut off separatist fighters. His force, along with others, came under fire from Russian troops and was encircled. When a sister battalion surrendered, he led some 260 troops back to Ukrainian lines.

His reputation rests on not just bravery but also compassion. In late 2024 he was appointed commander of the ground forces, a role focused on training and preparing troops, rather than leading them in battle. His first orders were aimed at improving their conditions, revamping recruitment and introducing technology to reduce losses. He also sought to implement a Western style of command, whereby subordinates were given more authority. “The command is gradually shifting from a culture of fear to a culture of responsibility,” he later wrote on Facebook. “For the first time, the initiative from below has ceased to be a threat, and has begun to become a resource.”

As he granted more responsibility, he held himself to the new standard. In 2025, after a Russian missile killed 12 soldiers on a training base, he resigned, saying he should be held accountable.

He was later deployed to a role in which he was more directly involved in planning combat operations, where he won the praise of his subordinate brigade commanders for listening to them and offering support. “He is a critic of Soviet-style thinking and micromanagement,” noted Rob Lee, an expert on the Ukraine war.

This approach was in stark contrast to that of General Syrsky, who was sacked by Volodymyr Zelensky, Ukraine’s president, amid big protests calling for him to go. General Syrsky had been unfairly nicknamed “the butcher”, partly because of the losses suffered during his dogged defence of the city of Bakhmut in 2023. Many commentators present the contrast between Generals Drapaty and Syrsky as a generational struggle between a young tech-savvy drone enthusiast and a Soviet-style traditionalist. But that misses the main points of difference between the two.

General Syrsky oversaw the widespread adoption of drones in the Ukrainian armed forces and the strategy of using medium-range drones to isolate Crimea and long-range drones to hit oil installations deep in Russia. Yet he also saw the value of investing resources in more traditional kit, such as tanks and artillery, since these are needed to blunt and break up attacks that would overwhelm defenders armed only with drones.

He is also seen as a talented tactical commander, who skilfully led the defence of Kyiv in 2022 and an offensive into Russian territory near Kursk two years later. The bigger concerns about General Syrsky’s leadership relate to what some saw as strategic blunders as well as favouritism in the allocation of reinforcements and other resources. Western officers involved in the planning of Ukraine’s big summer offensive in 2023 accused him of diverting troops to Bakhmut instead of concentrating forces for an attack in the south. Allies of the general counter that he was tying down Russian troops and that, if there was any misallocation of forces, blame for that should fall on Valery Zaluzhny, who was the chief commander at the time.

General Syrsky also developed a reputation for micromanagement and a refusal to fully accept the authority of the defence minister, Mykhailo Fedorov, another young moderniser. When Mr Fedorov tried to consolidate weak and poorly led units, General Syrsky formed new brigades, diluting already-scarce manpower. “Syrsky took several of Ukraine’s best units and deployed them as a split formation across opposite ends of the front,” wrote Jack Watling of the Royal United Services Institute, a think-tank in London.

After clashing with General Syrsky and failing to oust him, Mr Fedorov was sacked on July 15th by Mr Zelensky. The move triggered the protests calling for General Syrsky to go—and for Mr Fedorov’s return. Mr Zelensky has reportedly offered Mr Fedorov a new job, though it is unclear whether he will take it. The spat has changed his relationship with Mr Zelensky, which was once trusting and loyal. The outcry over Mr Fedorov’s sacking and its chaotic aftermath has hurt the president’s authority. The demonstrations included soldiers such as Andriy Syry, aged 27, who lost his foot in a drone strike. He attached a banner to his crutch reading: “I can’t stand up but I won’t shut up.” Whatever the talents of the new commander-in-chief, the problems he faces have no easy fix. ■

item.title: Dismissing Europe as a museum is glib. Think of it as a theme park
item.description:
Europe

Europe | Charlemagne How better to come under the spell of Mitteleuropa than to stroll across the Charles Bridge, admiring Prague’s baroque skyline before reaching the glistening cobblestones of its old town? If Gallic charm is your thing, surely nothing can be so Parisian as whiling away an af...
item.content:encoded:
Dismissing Europe as a museum is glib. Think of it as a theme park

Europe | Charlemagne


How better to come under the spell of Mitteleuropa than to stroll across the Charles Bridge, admiring Prague’s baroque skyline before reaching the glistening cobblestones of its old town? If Gallic charm is your thing, surely nothing can be so Parisian as whiling away an afternoon at the Café de Flore in Saint-Germain-des-Prés, where Jean-Paul Sartre once puffed on Gitanes as he pondered being and nothingness. Or one might seek to discover the ancestral essence of Europe by basking in the old-money haunt of Capri, the whitewashed Aegean island of Santorini, or the honey-coloured streets of Dubrovnik. Pick among these destinations wisely and Europe offers the discerning traveller an unrivalled chance to commune with the continent’s timeless soul.

Kidding! It has been decades since any local has even given thought to lingering in what were once the most charming parts of the continent. The Charles Bridge is merely a thoroughfare between tourist traps, the Flore is a relic best left to Instagrammers these days, Dubrovnik merely an entry on a visiting American’s bucket list. From Barcelona to Bruges by way of Florence, vast swathes of Europe’s once-idyllic cities are a procession of foreigners shopping for souvenirs. Some hilltop villages in Provence or Tuscany now seem to exist chiefly as backdrops for linen-clad types sipping spritzes. This counts as an economic success of sorts: a continent that struggles to export cars or chemicals now gets its dollars and yuan by enticing foreigners to come over and spend on its shores instead. Alas, that comes at a steep price. In summer Europeans are not so much residents of their home cities as extras in someone else’s social-media feed.

Forget the gibes about the old continent being a museum in which Europeans can live out their unambitious dolce vita. These days it is better to think of it as a theme park where locals can be gawped at by holidaying voyeurs. Museums preserve history; theme parks offer any visiting punter willing to suspend disbelief that feeling of being part of it. This is closer to the European tourist experience. For the point of a family holiday to France or Spain is not just to admire the scenery. It is also to imagine oneself a true European, a temporary denizen of the world’s lifestyle superpower. Indulging in long lunches, strolling through cities and dealing with surly waiters are just as much part of the travel experience as visiting the Uffizi. The continent’s greatest attraction is the suspicion that its inhabitants have somehow arranged life better.

Any European tempted to be flattered should remember that being a lifestyle superpower is not nearly the same as being the real thing. But hold that thought for after summer. Until then, selling authenticity by the night is a tidy earner. While America flogs artificial-intelligence models and China monopolises critical materials, only Charlemagne’s cramped peninsula seems to be able to satisfy the global middle class’s wanderlust. Of the roughly 1.5bn tourist journeys each year that involve crossing borders, over half are in European countries—a staggering success for a place with but a tenth of the world’s population. Six of the world’s ten most-visited countries are in Europe (including trips taken by fellow Europeans). The hotels, campsites and Airbnbs in the European Union can put up 32m people, enough to host the entire population of a dozen countries in the bloc. The nearly $900bn in revenues from international tourism make up around 7% of Europe’s exports, says the UN’s tourism arm. Who needs big tech when you have the Eiffel Tower and the Parthenon? Europe cannot create its own Google, but it excels at tempting Silicon Valley engineers into spending $1,500 a night to sleep in a converted convent. Would you like to see the gluten-free menu, madame?

Not every part of Europe partakes in the bonanza: the crowds remain unsurprisingly concentrated in a handful of photogenic bottlenecks. At the bustling end of the spectrum, even those who once welcomed well-heeled foreigners now realise they may have been too much of a good thing. Tourism hotspots in Spain and Croatia have been rebelling for a while, griping that short-term accommodation has turned homes into hotel rooms and residents into commuters. (Visiting Americans cosplaying at being European are often imitating locals who cannot themselves afford a break: for all their paid holiday, half of all Europeans lack the money for an annual trip of more than four days away from home.) Hoteliers and exchequers hooked on foreign income think the situation can be managed by shuffling visitors to more out-of-the-way places, or into quieter parts of the year. But imposing a tourism tax on hotels or trying to nudge tourists into the off-season won’t reclaim the Café de Flore for Parisians. Those days are gone.

Wary of anything that smells like economic success, Europe is currently busy undermining itself as a destination. One issue is bureaucracy, a recurring continental passion. The ham-fisted introduction of a new procedure to check passports for visitors to the EU has left many tourists this summer in airport queues lasting up to five hours. A more enduring problem is heatwaves. A little sweating was once part of the charm of visiting the continent’s southern shores, a nudge towards taking up local siesta habits. Now it feels stifling. Italy risks turning its peak summer season into an endurance test with gelato in lieu of air-conditioning.

Yet even that won’t deter the hordes. And so the great European summer shuffle will continue, as this former Parisian can attest. Those who can afford to leave the tourism-worthy bits of the city decamp to the beach. The resulting void is filled by foreigners who soon grumble about how many other foreigners are in this place. And thus, paradoxically, visitors get what is the authentic Parisian experience: sitting beside other tourists, and doing their utmost to pretend they are not there. ■

item.title: Beware of new prime ministers bearing gifts
item.description:
Britain

Britain | Enter Andy Britain’s new prime minister has inherited a country in a funk—and a Labour Party in a slump. On taking office on July 20th, Andy Burnham showed he could tap into the mood of a nation which needs a lift, and a party which needs a fresh start. Speaking in Downing Street, he ...
item.content:encoded:
Beware of new prime ministers bearing gifts

Britain | Enter Andy


Britain’s new prime minister has inherited a country in a funk—and a Labour Party in a slump. On taking office on July 20th, Andy Burnham showed he could tap into the mood of a nation which needs a lift, and a party which needs a fresh start. Speaking in Downing Street, he declared: “Let us make this the moment when Britain starts to believe again.”

Britons are feeling pessimistic about their future. Nearly-two thirds believe the country is heading in the wrong direction, according to polling by Ipsos. This gloomy outlook has persisted since the covid-19 pandemic gave way to a spike in inflation more than four years ago, and Mr Burnham’s four predecessors struggled to shift it. Gathering his cabinet for the first time on July 21st, the prime minister told his team they needed to “take that little bit of pressure off people’s shoulders”.

Mr Burnham is a good communicator; that is why Labour MPs are excited about a change from the stolid Sir Keir Starmer. Alas, his rhetoric has not been matched by a transformative vision for government. Sixteen years after he first tried to become party leader, and a year since he began planning for his new job in earnest, Mr Burnham has hit the ground strolling.

He told his cabinet to be “boldly Labour”, and has railed against 40 years of “neoliberalism” which he claims have devastated parts of Britain, particularly in his home region of the north of England. Mr Burnham has hinted at support for transformative (but probably self-defeating) policies such as wealth taxes, rent controls, the nationalisation of utilities and constitutional reform. None of those, however, made it into his initial policy programme, which is almost entirely short-termist.

Instead, Mr Burnham set out policies of limited ambition designed to fulfil a promise to lead “a cost-of-living government”, although wage stagnation, not inflation (which has fallen to 2.6%), is now the biggest constraint on living standards. He cut value-added tax on energy bills from 5% to zero and reintroduced a cap of £2 ($2.67) on bus fares throughout England (other than London, where fares are already cheaper). For businesses, he has promised a discount on the local taxes of certain types of pubs and bars.

The energy announcement was only a modest advance on similar moves by Sir Keir, while the bus cap is a return to an identical policy in place under the previous Conservative government. Both policies will expire within a year of coming into force, and the promised sources of funding look questionable. Previous such small-scale attempts to make life more affordable have not won over voters. Mr Burnham presumably hopes that by setting them out as his very first moves he will convince the public that the long squeeze on their incomes is at last coming to an end.

Although Mr Burnham declared he was “ready”, he has signalled that some of his biggest decisions will be kicked down the road. He has promised to produce a “ten-year plan” sometime in the autumn. This is likely to include his solution to the knotty problem of how to reform social care for the elderly. His biggest policy passion is the devolution of power from Westminster to the English regions, but even there he has provided little detail beyond setting up a “Number 10 North” office in Manchester. Several Starmer-era policies, including the proposed handover of the Chagos Islands to Mauritius and a plan to restrict the number of jury trials in order to speed up the courts, are now under review.

As well as boldness on policy, Mr Burnham pledged a politics of unity and an end to Labour’s sniping between factions. That remains to be seen. Mr Burnham immediately fired from the cabinet most of those involved in crafting Sir Keir’s approach to the economy, which (in rhetoric if not always in practice) favoured tech, deregulation and a focus on housebuilding in order to gee up Britain’s sluggish growth.

Rachel Reeves was sacked as chancellor. Peter Kyle, Steve Reed, Liz Kendall and Darren Jones were removed from their posts overseeing, respectively, business, housing, science and the machinery of government. Other casualties included those whose only fault was loyalty to the last prime minister, such as Sir Keir’s deputy, David Lammy. The potential problems with this approach became apparent straight away, as Mr Jones went public with criticism of Mr Burnham’s unfunded spending promises.

By contrast, those Labour bigwigs who had fallen out with the previous regime were rewarded with promotions. Chief among these are the new chancellor, John Healey, who resigned as defence secretary in June after a row over funding, and Wes Streeting, who called for Sir Keir to go and is now in charge of defence. Angela Rayner, Louise Haigh and Lucy Powell—all fired by Sir Keir at some point—are back in senior positions. Ministers who let it be known that they had privately told Sir Keir to quit have either kept their jobs (such as Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary) or landed a promotion (such as Ed Miliband, who becomes foreign secretary). Mr Burnham’s commitment to healing old wounds in his party looks shaky.

Mr Healey’s return to the Treasury, where he served as a junior minister in the government of Sir Tony Blair two decades ago, is a welcome signal that Mr Burnham’s assault on economic orthodoxy will go only so far. The new chancellor told the cabinet that “we need to look hard at our own budgets”; given his previous role he is expected to prioritise defence for any new public-spending splurge. Pat McFadden, the flinty work-and-pensions secretary, stays in place, suggesting that efforts to bear down on the welfare bill will continue. Mr Burnham has abolished the standalone department for science and technology, a decision opposed by the tech industry, but made up for it by giving Kanishka Narayan, the AI minister, a seat at the cabinet table.

In his first week, the prime minister has preferred quick wins to starting work on the long-term reforms needed to restore Britain to health—and see off the populism of left and right. Though he had friendly phone calls with Donald Trump and other world leaders, his views on foreign policy remain murky. He has said almost nothing about his policy on immigration, the topic which—along with the economy—will decide the next election. He is sending mixed messages on whether he will continue the baleful trend of shifting the tax burden towards higher earners while prioritising pensioners for handouts.

This vagueness leaves Mr Burnham wriggle room to take his government in a more adventurous direction. So far, the early signs are that he is falling short of his grander promises. ■

item.title: Andy Burnham’s first decisions in office reveal a lot about him
item.description:
Britain

Britain | Calorific canapés In his first days as prime minister, Andy Burnham presented his amuse-bouches to the British public. He announced that VAT, a consumption tax, would be cut on electricity bills from 5% to 0% from October. The cap on most bus fares would be slashed from £3 ($4) to £2 ...
item.content:encoded:
Andy Burnham’s first decisions in office reveal a lot about him

Britain | Calorific canapés


In his first days as prime minister, Andy Burnham presented his amuse-bouches to the British public. He announced that VAT, a consumption tax, would be cut on electricity bills from 5% to 0% from October. The cap on most bus fares would be slashed from £3 ($4) to £2 for all of 2027. From April, pubs and clubs in England will get a 20% business-rate cut. Mr Burnham’s portion sizes are meagre: the electricity tax cut will save just £25 per household in this tax year, according to the Institute for Fiscal Studies, a think-tank.

These tasters show Mr Burnham’s strengths. He is a more political animal than Sir Keir Starmer, his predecessor, and understands that tackling the cost of living will be crucial for his success. Unfortunately, he has served up policies that resemble baked Camemberts: they have lots of fatty calories and are liable to cause indigestion later on.

The calorie count is large and growing. Cutting electricity bills costs £850m this tax year alone. Mr Burnham says he will fund it by scrapping Sir Keir’s scheme to introduce digital IDs. But that policy was unfunded, so in reality he will need to find the cash elsewhere. It will be hard to ransack energy budgets, as he has already raided them for £454m to help fund the bus-fare cuts. These early decisions reflect Mr Burnham’s big-spending instincts. If he is not careful, the state’s waistline could balloon.

Nor are Mr Burnham’s offerings nutritious. By capping bus fares nationally, he is taking away the agency of mayors to decide how to support their bus networks. That’s the opposite of the devolution dream he ostensibly espouses. He is also blunting price signals.

The electricity tax cut is poorly targeted: richer households will save the most money. And the scrapped digital-ID scheme would in time have made it much easier to use public services. These are ominous signs of a short-termist leader ducking hard decisions.

Mr Burnham says these moves show his promise to “bring back hope”. But the most disgruntled diner is one who gets excited by the menu but disappointed by the food. The best way to tackle the cost of living is to get real wages rising through growth. If Mr Burnham is distracted by £25 giveaways, not even his communication skills will save him. ■

item.title: How Britain’s new prime minister can revive Labour
item.description:
Britain

Britain | Feel the Burn Labour MPs hope that by picking the former mayor of Greater Manchester to replace Sir Keir Starmer they can clean the slate after two troubled years in power. Opinion polls suggest they may be right—at least for now. Andy Burnham is more popular than Sir Keir (a low bar)...
item.content:encoded:
How Britain’s new prime minister can revive Labour

Britain | Feel the Burn


Labour MPs hope that by picking the former mayor of Greater Manchester to replace Sir Keir Starmer they can clean the slate after two troubled years in power. Opinion polls suggest they may be right—at least for now.

Andy Burnham is more popular than Sir Keir (a low bar), but he also has better ratings than the now-departed prime minister had two years ago, when he came to power. Sir Keir squandered the political capital he had at astonishing speed with a series of u-turns and reinventions that voters hated. Though Mr Burnham’s popularity may be equally short-lived, the data suggest that the new Labour leader could build a more enduring electoral base by uniting Britain’s fragmented centre-left voters.

To dig into Mr Burnham’s base of support, The Economist analysed a survey of 5,070 Britons conducted by Stack Data Strategy, a polling firm, between July 7th and 14th. The pollster asked respondents which party they would vote for if an election were held tomorrow. It then repeated the question, asking respondents to consider how they would vote if Mr Burnham were leader of the Labour Party as well as prime minister. The effect was to add 2.1 percentage points to Labour’s vote share—a small but meaningful improvement (see map).

The new prime minister has tied his political identity to the north of England. Northerners have noticed. Across the region Labour’s vote share under Mr Burnham improves by around six points. In his stomping-ground around Manchester the improvement is closer to ten points—not to be sniffed at. Only 26% of seats in Parliament are in the north of England, but over the past decade the region has been rising in political salience. The Economist’s election model suggests that around 45% of the marginal constituencies which Labour needs to win for a parliamentary majority are in the north.

Mr Burnham’s northern roots are also an asset in Britain’s fraught class system. Despite his relatively comfortable upbringing (his father was a BT engineer, his mother a doctor’s receptionist) followed by a degree at Cambridge University, around 46% of Britons say that Mr Burnham is working-class. That compares with only 14% for Sir Keir, the son of a toolmaker, and 18% for the former health secretary (and new defence secretary), Wes Streeting, who was brought up by a single mother in an east London council flat. According to Stack’s data, replacing Sir Keir with Mr Burnham would leave Labour’s vote share unchanged among respondents in the most middle-class occupations, while increasing it by 3.6 percentage points among those in the most working-class jobs.

With Mr Burnham’s northern, working-class hue, some commentators mistakenly believe that he is particularly appealing to supporters of the populist-right Reform UK party (many of whom are northern or working-class). In Stack’s polling, however, just 2% of Reform supporters switch to Labour when Mr Burnham is listed as party leader—compared with 4% of Liberal Democrats, 5% of Conservatives and 6% of Green supporters. According to YouGov, another pollster, Mr Burnham has a net favourability rating of +20 points among Green supporters and +21 among Liberal Democrats, compared with a dismal -62 among Reform supporters (see chart). The same voters gave Sir Keir ratings of -47, -14 and -92, respectively.

Faced with this evidence, Mr Burnham might be encouraged to tack to his left, attempting to unite Britain’s broadly left-of-centre bloc in order to defeat Reform. But such an approach brings risks. The first is that left-wing voters tend to be concentrated in relatively few constituencies. Judging by current polls, most Labour MPs could face Reform as the leading challenger in their constituencies. In these contests, switchers from Reform to Labour are in effect worth double.

The second risk is that left-wing voters might not reward Mr Burnham for left-wing policies. There is little evidence that Sir Keir’s most left-leaning policies have won him any friends. His approach—presenting himself as a moderate while pursuing a solidly centre-left agenda—has alienated voters to both his left and right.

In this respect, Mr Burnham begins his time in Downing Street with a head start. Before becoming prime minister, Sir Keir had to contort himself in order to be elected Labour leader by the party’s left-wing membership. As leader of the opposition, he then strained to persuade voters that he was in fact a moderate who had changed the Labour Party. Finally, in government, he had to satisfy the demands of left-wing backbenchers. The whiplash was too much: by May 2026 nearly three-quarters of Britons thought the prime minister was indecisive, according to YouGov. By contrast, voters are still open to finding out what Mr Burnham stands for.

His first electoral test will come sooner than most predecessors’. On July 30th voters in Greater Manchester will elect Mr Burnham’s successor as mayor. Reform won the region with a clear margin in May’s local elections, but polls now suggest that Labour’s candidate—an ally of Mr Burnham—is on course for victory. It would be a good start for Labour. ■

item.title: Tours of British post-war housing are a quiet hit
item.description:
Britain

Britain | Grey expectations Langham House Close is the sort of place often passed without a second look. A cluster of low apartment blocks of sandy brick and exposed concrete slabs, it is tucked behind a much grander Georgian mansion which gives it its name. But to the informed visitor, brought b...
item.content:encoded:
Tours of British post-war housing are a quiet hit

Britain | Grey expectations


Langham House Close is the sort of place often passed without a second look. A cluster of low apartment blocks of sandy brick and exposed concrete slabs, it is tucked behind a much grander Georgian mansion which gives it its name. But to the informed visitor, brought by their paper walking-guide to the suburb of Ham in south-west London, it reveals architectural genius. “Note the jutting concrete ‘gargoyles’, inspired by Le Corbusier’s Maison Jaoul,” the guide instructs, of the at-first-glance unremarkable gutter spouts. This was an early work (from 1958) of James Stirling and James Gowan, who would become stars of post-war architecture. Its style became known as “new brutalism” and inspired a generation of British housing.

Finding the poetry in buildings for years dismissed as totalitarian, or plain ugly, is the work of “Perambulations”, a series of walking tours of modernist homes. Their quiet success reflects a wider rehabilitation of ideas about architecture found across the rich world in the decades after the second world war. “Perambulations” started as a pandemic project of Stefi Orazi, a graphic designer, who logged her daily walks around north London’s modernist houses on social media. Set to two sides of paper, a first print run quickly sold out. The series is now on its 30th issue, with more than 40,000 copies sold.

Her typical self-guided tour takes in a couple of dozen properties, mostly in London but also Cambridge, Berlin, Brussels and Paris. Some stops are famous, now found on tea towels and posters. They include the Trellick Tower (in guide number 9), a brutalist monolith in west London designed by Erno Goldfinger. Ian Fleming, an author, so disliked the family home Goldfinger built in Willow Road, Hampstead (guide no 2), that he immortalised the architect as the villain of a James Bond novel.

Others are the early works of future superstars, such as a modest row of mews houses in Kentish Town by Norman Foster and Richard Rogers, who would go on to redraw the skylines of Europe. But the most interesting are the family homes commissioned by middle-class doctors and academics from largely forgotten architects. Ms Orazi’s aim, in part, was to create a historical record. She scours council archives for original plans. “I sometimes think, if I don’t write about them, maybe they never will be [written about].”

Britons enjoy nosying at the homes of their neighbours. But another attraction is the guides’ old-fashioned rigour, an antidote to the age of Instagram. They are printed in two-tone ink with small photographs and dense text. Note, they instruct, how the house numbers are set into the brickwork, and the shape of the decorative lintels. Readers who do not know their pilotis from their paviours soon learn.

Interest in post-war architecture picked up a decade ago as people became worried about the scale of Britain’s current housing shortage, reckons Ms Orazi. The haste to rebuild bombed-out British cities created a legion of opponents; it increasingly looks like a feat worth replicating. For those struggling to raise a deposit for a flat, peering at a family home in north London might produce the same vicarious daydreams as a tour of a country estate.

There is a lot of concrete. But it is not all drab. Take the Alexandra Road estate in Swiss Cottage. Palms and lush climbers spill over the terraced balconies; on a hot July day you might be in Caracas. Or Parkleys, in Ham, built by Eric Lyons’s firm, Span, in the 1950s. The freshly painted olive-green panels, red hung tiling and angular white canopies over the footpaths are as jaunty as if they were made from Lego.

For traditionalists like King Charles, modernist architecture is oppressive, attempting to override the “inner world of humanity” with machine-like rationalism, as he once put it. The architects saw it otherwise: their buildings were stripped of ornament precisely because they prioritised the people inside them. Ms Orazi’s own home in north London, built in the 1970s to designs by Gordon Benson and Alan Forsyth (guide no 3), gives little away on the outside: a long, white building with narrow windows like the slots of a pillbox. But inside the apartments are airy, with split-level floors and huge skylights. “They were designing from the inside out,” she says. “The outside is just a consequence of trying to rationalise the inside.”

There were remarkable opportunities for young architects. Peter Tabori, a Hungarian émigré, was 28 when he was put in charge of Highgate New Town, in north London, which resembles a Tuscan hill town. Not far away is 62 Camden Mews, the family home of Ted Cullinan, an architect (guide no 15). He built it at weekends on a scrap of derelict land with the help of friends; bricks were salvaged from his day job working for Denys Lasdun, the designer of the National Theatre. With heavy black timber frames, angular eaves, a shaded courtyard and entry to the upper floor over something resembling a drawbridge, it is a tranquil pocket of Kyoto on a London backstreet. A smartly positioned letter box drops the Sunday papers into the adults’ bedroom. It sold for more than £900,000 ($1.2m) last year.

Today’s planning system might have suffocated it at birth. Loaded with red tape and vetoes, it rewards safety-firstism, and deters experimentation. It is intended to prevent clunkers; it also weeds out genius. But when cities are free to build, they will often produce delights.■

item.title: Britons are increasingly tussling over inheritance
item.description:
Britain

Britain | Family fortunes When there’s a will, there’s a war. Or so they say in the courts of England and Wales, which are growing busier with fights over the dead’s estates. The number of probate claims listed at the High Court has grown by over 400% over the past decade, according to Solomoni...
item.content:encoded:
Britons are increasingly tussling over inheritance

Britain | Family fortunes


When there’s a will, there’s a war. Or so they say in the courts of England and Wales, which are growing busier with fights over the dead’s estates. The number of probate claims listed at the High Court has grown by over 400% over the past decade, according to Solomonic, a legal-analytics company. The first three months of this year saw the highest number filed during any quarter on record. With most disputes over estates settled out of court, this is the tip of the iceberg.

Several factors explain the rise in family fisticuffs. Whereas most of the rest of Europe has “forced heirship” systems, which guarantee spouses and children a fixed share of an estate, in England, Wales and Northern Ireland you can disinherit anyone you like—on whatever grounds you like. Yet at the same time the law in those jurisdictions gives a wide cast of characters—from spouses to stepchildren to financial dependents—a route to challenge a will if they can show they were left without “reasonable financial provision”. As family structures have become both looser and more complex, this has left more people feeling that they might have a right to a slice of the cake.

Demography makes matters worse. Britons are living longer but with conditions (particularly dementia) that can reduce their ability to make sound decisions, prompting more disputes over whether the deceased even had capacity to execute a will. Meanwhile, young people are increasingly reliant on their inheritance to get onto the property ladder: the average age of first-time buyers recently rose to 34 in England, with nearly one in three deposits coming from family gifts, and almost a tenth from inheritance.

The stakes are higher too: the money people stand to inherit—or lose—has never been greater. The government’s tax authority collected a record £8.5bn ($11.5bn, or 0.3% of GDP) in inheritance-tax receipts over the 2025-26 tax year. With thresholds frozen since 2009, and house prices up by more than 70% since then, more estates are being pulled in. Britain’s new prime minister previously suggested he would replace inheritance tax with a progressive “care levy” that everyone would pay, which would make more estates liable.

“There used to be a concern that it was bad form to sue your own relatives. But that is gone,” says Paul Grimwood of Knights, a law firm. He thinks litigiousness has been normalised by TV shows such as “Inheritance Wars”, a Channel 5 documentary series, and tabloid coverage of feuding families. Nearly four in ten respondents to a survey conducted last year by Level Group, a British probate-lending firm, said they would go to court over unexpected or unfair inheritance.

Lawyers expect the uptick in probate disputes to continue. AI-drafted wills are another reason. According to a survey commissioned by the Association of Lifetime Lawyers, an industry training network, 72% of Britons aged 30 to 34 would consider using AI for will-writing. Jessica Medus of Mishcon de Reya, another law firm, says there is a “a genuine access-to-justice argument”; if AI tools prompt more people to think about estate planning, “that is a positive”. But like most litigators, she is mainly worried about the risks. Poorly drafted wills are already a leading cause of disputes; AI chatbots’ tendency towards vague language could produce more.

All this means lawyers dealing with wills, trusts and estates are becoming busier, and more numerous. Irwin Mitchell, which claims to be one of the largest law firms in the field, has twice as many people working in it as a decade ago. With an estimated £5.5trn expected to pass between generations by 2050, the business is unlikely to slow down. For the families involved, any victory is often pyrrhic. The cruellest inheritance may be a legal bill.■

item.title: Postcard from the Liz Truss festival of ideas
item.description:
Britain

Britain | The populist right “Disappointing” and “shit” was how some attendees summarised the inaugural CPAC GB conference in Greenwich on July 16th-18th. The event, hosted by Liz Truss, Britain’s shortest-serving prime minister, was inspired by America’s influential Conservative Political Acti...
item.content:encoded:
Postcard from the Liz Truss festival of ideas

Britain | The populist right


“Disappointing” and “shit” was how some attendees summarised the inaugural CPAC GB conference in Greenwich on July 16th-18th. The event, hosted by Liz Truss, Britain’s shortest-serving prime minister, was inspired by America’s influential Conservative Political Action Conference. Intended as a show of strength for the new right in Britain, it was an advert for its weakness.

Worse than the empty seats were the empty ideas. If CPAC GB was your introduction to British politics, you would come away thinking that Sir Keir Starmer was a communist and that the country is ruled by a sinister coalition of jihadis and “homo-Leninists” funded by George Soros and the Fabian Society (a left-leaning think-tank increasingly singled out as the force shaping Soviet Britain).

In principle CPAC exists to provide a platform for conservatives to share ideas. Britain’s instalment felt more like a Reform UK rally. Its leader, Nigel Farage, who pulled by far the biggest crowd, used his platform to slate both the Conservative Party and Restore Britain, a breakaway far-right party. But in the foyer disgruntled attendees questioned why Tommy Robinson and Restore’s leader, Rupert Lowe, hadn’t been invited.

Britain is often downstream of America, in culture as in politics. But at CPAC GB some of the Yankification fell flat. Daily prayers were sparsely attended. The sponsors were mostly American. Documents seen by the Guardian suggest that the Trump administration intends to allocate $12m ($16m) to British-based conservative groups, including some founded by CPAC GB speakers.

Whether Ms Truss and her fellow-travellers truly believe the paranoid MAGA worldview preached in Greenwich, or whether they just need the money, is hard to say. For all her efforts, the carnival vibe and colourful costumes that define America’s CPAC were missing. In her closing remarks, Ms Truss described how taken she was by the American version of the event. “An experience”, she said, “you will never experience anywhere else.” How right she was. ■

item.title: If Andy Burnham is going to achieve big things, he has to act now
item.description:
Britain

Britain | Bagehot Changing prime minister has become an all too familiar ceremony. On July 20th Sir Keir Starmer bade farewell and zipped from Downing Street to Buckingham Palace, with helicopters hovering above. Andy Burnham, the new prime minister, followed in reverse, heading from Buckingham...
item.content:encoded:
If Andy Burnham is going to achieve big things, he has to act now

Britain | Bagehot


Changing prime minister has become an all too familiar ceremony. On July 20th Sir Keir Starmer bade farewell and zipped from Downing Street to Buckingham Palace, with helicopters hovering above. Andy Burnham, the new prime minister, followed in reverse, heading from Buckingham Palace to Downing Street, where friends, family, allies and apparatchiks listened to his hopes for Britain.

Then began the next stage: picking over every word. What did Mr Burnham mean when he called his government a “circuit-breaker”? Was his target to eliminate rough sleeping feasible? And most important: what will Mr Burnham do in his first 100 days?

At this point, the chuntering starts. Why judge a government that will run the country for years after only 100 days? Forget the first days, what about the next ten years? What better symbol of the adhd-addled media environment that makes governing impossible? But whereas most media conventions can be dismissed, the first-100-days meme cannot. It reflects a fundamental truth of British politics. The most consequential government actions happen almost immediately or not at all.

Take Sir Tony Blair. Practically all New Labour’s lasting achievements happened within days of taking power. Bank of England independence, which is now the backbone of British economic policy, came on day five. A plan to give Scotland and Wales their own parliaments, on day 14. By the end of the first month, the national minimum wage was in progress. After eight weeks, what became the Human Rights Act was outlined. To round off this busy first 100 days, plans for a London mayor were unveiled.

What about the next dozen years? Oh, they did this and that. Public services improved; waiting lists fell, eventually. Schools were rebuilt; the public realm was renewed. But this was temporary, as a trip down any high street or a visit to hospital today will show. New Labour’s achievements faded away and Sir Tony, the most successful prime minister of the past 30 years, spent two decades kicking himself for not doing more sooner.

And so it was for the Conservative-Liberal Democrat coalition government led by David Cameron that took power in 2010. Austerity was put in train at once; the government announced it would crank vat to its current level of 20% after a little over a month. The triple lock, which guarantees that the state pension must rise by the rate of inflation, wage growth or 2.5%, came on the 42nd day of the Cameron era. A good 16 years on, it is still there, a symbol of the long-term unseriousness of British policy, since it will eventually lead to the heat-death of the fiscal universe unless someone tweaks it.

By 2014 the legislative cupboard was almost bare. Critics called it a zombie parliament. Whips desperately emailed MPs for ideas for debates. (Perhaps food security? What about foreign lorries?) When Mr (now Lord) Cameron won a majority in the 2015 election, he set Brexit in train almost immediately. He produced the referendum bill on the eu on day 21, sealing his government’s fate.

Likewise, Theresa May took her biggest decisions within weeks of winning power. At her first Conservative Party conference as leader, Mrs (now Lady) May set Britain on a path to a hard Brexit. Her place in history was secured by day 82. It took Boris Johnson a bit longer to rejig Britain’s relationship with Europe: he reached a deal with the eu on day 86, which was one half of his legacy. The other half was a boom in immigration. When did Mr Johnson ditch the Conservative Party’s long-held pledge to cut immigration to “tens of thousands”? Day one.

Most governments take up to 100 days or so to shape a country. Liz Truss managed it in half that. She pledged energy subsidies roughly equivalent to the annual British defence budget. When a ragbag of sweeping tax cuts were thrown in, markets moved, Tory mps followed and Ms Truss was gone. Unpicking that budget was Rishi Sunak’s job, which he did in the first few weeks. Grill veterans of the Sunak era about their achievements and at the top comes the Windsor Framework, which restored relations between the eu and Britain to normalcy, and dominated the start of Mr Sunak’s tenure. Little else matters from Mr Sunak’s stint.

What happens when a government fails to sprint at the start? Ask drinkers at The Grafton, a pub in north London, which on July 20th hosted relieved and humiliated members of Sir Keir’s team, who toasted their freedom from the burdens of government barely two years after a landslide victory.

Of all the sins of Sir Keir’s time in office, it was the start that proved mortal. In the first 100 days of Sir Keir’s tenure there was a great vacuum where a government should be. In the time that other governments had begun upending Britain’s constitution or ripping through the country’s fiscal position or taking Britain out of Europe, Sir Keir cut winter-fuel payments to pensioners, embroiled himself in a scandal about the number of freebies he accepted and sacked his chief of staff. After barely two months in power, prescient obituaries of “two-year Keir” were written, even if they felt absurd at the time.

First impressions are usually correct. Governments do not change much in office. Errors compound and events scar them, but their basic instincts and flaws remain the same. To the extent that prime ministers control their destiny at all, they control their first few months. And so the most significant period of Mr Burnham’s government has already begun. A strategy for the next decade is coming, says Mr Burnham, but in the autumn. Judging by his predecessors, it could well be too late. They had already been assigned their place in history by that point. If Mr Burnham has a plan, Britain needs to hear it soon, or it never will. ■

item.title: The Iran war is consuming the Trump presidency
item.description:
International

International | The Telegram HERE IS A thought to chill the blood of President Donald Trump. He would be in a far better place today if he had followed the foreign-policy advice of the predecessor he loathes, Barack Obama. According to the Obama doctrine, as explained years ago to Jeffrey Goldb...
item.content:encoded:
The Iran war is consuming the Trump presidency

International | The Telegram


HERE IS A thought to chill the blood of President Donald Trump. He would be in a far better place today if he had followed the foreign-policy advice of the predecessor he loathes, Barack Obama. According to the Obama doctrine, as explained years ago to Jeffrey Goldberg, a journalist, an American president’s first duty in world affairs is: “Don’t do stupid shit.”

As doctrines go, it is not very sophisticated. Moreover, cerebral Mr Obama left a mixed foreign-policy record: he was slow to grasp the full scope of the China threat, for instance. Still, if Mr Trump had heeded him, he might not have joined Israel in launching war on Iran on February 28th without a plan for victory. Mr Trump might not have boasted that the killing of Iran’s top leaders, followed by punishing air strikes, would soon trigger regime change. Given Iran’s complexity and its rulers’ ruthlessness, that was as daft as predicting that the Mafia could be bombed out of Sicily from the air. Now, Mr Trump’s war may consume his presidency.

The president’s Middle East record includes real successes, notably the recognition of Israel by four Arab states in the Abraham accords. Mr Trump deserves credit for (belatedly) strong-arming Israel’s prime minister, Binyamin Netanyahu, into a ceasefire last year with Hamas, though conditions in Gaza remain grim. His decision to join Israel in bombarding Iran’s nuclear sites last summer was risky, but not stupid. The operation came with costs, including the loss of access to Iran’s highly enriched uranium for international inspectors. Still, inflicting severe damage on Iran’s underground nuclear programme followed a coherent logic. Iran’s muted response in retaliation was a further vindication.

Not all presidential blunders meet the Obama-doctrine test. Take Mr Trump’s repeated demands to own Greenland. He is deeply unwise to alienate Denmark, the island’s colonial master and a devoted American friend. Still, Denmark remains a NATO ally, needing America to deter Russia. In contrast, an actual invasion of Greenland would qualify as unambiguously stupid shit.

When Mr Obama coined the term, he was thinking of his own predecessor, George Bush, and the fatal mix of vengefulness, impatience and over-ambition that doomed the American-led campaigns in Afghanistan and Iraq that followed the September 2001 terrorist attacks. After studying the Bush years, Mr Obama learned (and indeed overlearned) abiding lessons about the dangers of American hubris. He was sceptical of nation-building in far-off lands, believed that only the gravest threats to America warrant armed intervention and thought of many allies as aggravating free-riders on American power. Striving to balance his coldly realist instincts with the liberal values that he believed his country should uphold, he suggested that America should pick its battles, and be “hardheaded at the same time as we’re bighearted”.

As it happens, Mr Trump shares many Obama-esque instincts, for all his sniping at the man. He too is wary of nation-building and annoyed by free-riding allies. He is unlike Mr Obama in his relish for America First bullying, his disastrous disdain for detail, his unblushing personal greed and his contempt for liberal values. In an unhappy mirror-image of the Obama years, Trumpian foreign policy too often revels in being bigheaded and hardhearted.

When it comes to the Middle East, both presidents hoped America could pivot away from a role as the region’s dominant security provider. From 2011 or so, the Obama administration openly sought to shift military and diplomatic resources away from Iraq and Afghanistan towards Asia, a dynamic region where investments of American power would “yield the biggest returns”. Obama aides talked of increased American energy production rendering the Middle East less relevant. With some bitterness, they accused such allies as Saudi Arabia of trying to goad America into fighting Iran on the Arab world’s behalf. Mr Obama’s full pivot to Asia was thwarted by renewed Middle Eastern instability, though, including civil war in Syria and the rise of Islamic State.

Mr Trump announced his own Middle Eastern pivot last year. The region would soon be “defined by commerce, not chaos”, he told Arab leaders in Riyadh. The days of the Middle East dominating American foreign policy are “thankfully over”, declared his national-security strategy, with conflict replaced by deals to sell American nuclear, defence and AI technologies. Seeking returns of their very own, Trump family members have secured hundreds of millions of dollars from Gulf rulers and their investment funds.

Then Mr Trump launched his war with Iran, upending Gulf business models. It is hard for Arab states to build billion-dollar data centres filled with American chips when Iranian missiles are falling. A different, gloomier sort of pivot now looms, involving Middle Eastern partners losing faith in America as a reliable ally.

Though the United Arab Emirates remains all-in on defence ties with America, others in the Gulf, led by Saudi Arabia, the regional giant, can be seen hedging. America remains uniquely important as a partner, but it is less trusted. Some Gulf rulers will quietly pay Iran for a quiet life. Others are deepening defence ties with such actors as Turkey, and economic links with China. It does not help that Mr Trump has played down Iranian attacks on American bases and local infrastructure in Gulf countries, anxious to obscure the war’s costs. Perhaps eager to convey his dominance as the war raged, in March Mr Trump publicly mocked the Saudi crown prince, Muhammad bin Salman, bragging that the prince never imagined “he’d be kissing my ass” as American president.

In a rough world brains are not everything, as the Obama administration learned to its chagrin. But Mr Obama was right that reckless presidential stupidity causes catastrophes. If Mr Trump talked less and listened more, he might have heard the warning. ■

item.title: The geopolitics of air-conditioning
item.description:
International

International | Trying to stay cool On a sun-baked morning in early July, with temperatures set to soar above 40°C (104°F), a mob in Nanterre, a Paris suburb, heaved against the doors of a Lidl supermarket until they collapsed. The sweat-stained hooligans were desperate shoppers, pitted against...
item.content:encoded:
The geopolitics of air-conditioning

International | Trying to stay cool


On a sun-baked morning in early July, with temperatures set to soar above 40°C (104°F), a mob in Nanterre, a Paris suburb, heaved against the doors of a Lidl supermarket until they collapsed. The sweat-stained hooligans were desperate shoppers, pitted against each other for the last portable air-conditioning (AC) unit. In another Lidl across town two men came to blows. French politicians had a row of their own, over how much AC was too much.

At about the same time in cities across Pakistan and Bangladesh, protesters blocked roads and surrounded electricity offices during weeks of power cuts in temperatures as hot as 45°C. In Chandpur, Bangladesh, in late June residents allegedly assaulted an employee of the Rural Electrification Board. In May power cuts during a heatwave in India led to similar protests in some rural villages, where residents complained they could not even run fans at night. In places like Iraq and Sri Lanka, too, unrest has broken out over shortages of energy needed to keep cool.

As extreme heat breaks tempers and electricity grids, fights over AC—or the energy that powers cooling tech—are threatening to break politics. It is a decidedly modern problem: AC hardly existed even in America before 1960; now climate change has made it a near-absolute must in much of the world. In November the COP30 climate summit, held in Belém, Brazil, declared cooling technologies like air-conditioning to be “essential infrastructure” like water, energy and sanitation.

Of all extreme weather, high temperatures are overwhelmingly the most deadly. Between 2000 and 2019 an estimated 489,000 people died of heat each year, according to modelling published in the Lancet, a medical journal. AC has proved a strikingly effective response. A separate study in the Lancet estimates that by the early 2020s AC was averting around 190,000 deaths each year in people aged 65 or older. In America researchers at the National Bureau of Economic Research reckon that residential AC was responsible for a roughly 75% decline over the 20th century in the risk of dying on a very hot day, defined as above 27°C on average. Almost all of that decline came after 1960, when American households began to adopt AC.

All that might seem to lead to a straightforward political calculus: more AC for everyone, everywhere. But it has not proved so simple. In rich countries politicians fight about climate and energy-efficiency. In poor countries, about the price of electricity, and ageing, rickety electric grids. And everywhere, they must contend with a public that increasingly expects, or outright demands, access to AC.

Take the rich countries first. Populist-right figures spy a clear opportunity in the hazy heat. In June Marine Le Pen, leader of France’s National Rally, demanded more air-conditioners in the country’s schools, hospitals and care homes. Jean-Luc Mélenchon, her rival on the populist left, countered that “air-conditioning everywhere” would heat up the planet, thereby only “increasing the damage”. Globally, cooling produces around 4% of greenhouse-gas emissions. The UN expects demand for AC and refrigeration to more than triple by 2050 on current trends, nearly doubling those emissions again.

Even in climate-controlled America, where 90% of households have AC, the MAGA right has tried to score cool points. On July 1st Zohran Mamdani, the Democratic Socialist mayor of New York, called on New Yorkers to set their AC to 78°F (26°C) to protect the power grid from overloading during a heatwave. Ted Cruz, a Republican senator from Texas, mockingly wrote in response, “In a first-world country you could turn on the AC…”. Others noted that Mr Cruz’s home state routinely issues the same guidance to protect its grid.

Ms Le Pen, at least, has more than populism on her side. Europe is both wealthy and temperate for its latitude. Yet it is, by a large margin, the region where heat kills most disproportionately, the Lancet model finds: 36% of the world’s heat deaths are attributed to Europe, which is home to less than 10% of the world’s people. And the annual death toll is rising. The World Health Organisation says it has gone up by 30% in two decades. Some of that is because Europeans are older, and the old are more vulnerable to heat.
